title: JWST Reveals Early Galaxies May Be 4x More Massive Than We Thought
summary:
Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) have made a startling discovery: some of the largest galaxies in the early universe may be far more massive than previously estimated. The findings, published in Nature Astronomy, could shake up our understanding of how the first galaxies formed.

An international team, including researchers from Penn State, examined nine massive, mature galaxies that stopped forming new stars billions of years ago. By combining JWST's infrared observations with ground-based data from the Very Large Telescope, they were able to estimate the relative numbers of small, faint stars versus large, bright ones.

"These galaxies are different," said Joel Leja, a coauthor and professor at Penn State. "They're different in the way that is really challenging to understand, because they are more massive than we expected -- like a lot more massive, they have three or four times more mass than we expected."

The challenge is that bright stars dominate the light we see, while smaller stars are much dimmer and harder to detect. Lead author Chloe Cheng compared it to a city: "If a galaxy were a city, the brightest stars would be the skyscrapers that immediately catch your eye from afar. Our models demonstrate that a far more numerous population of low-mass stars is concealed by those rare, bright stars, like houses hidden between skyscrapers."

One galaxy stood out: it formed less than 1.5 billion years after the Big Bang and could be up to four times more massive than previous calculations suggested. Coauthor Martje Slob noted, "Until recently, measurements like these were simply impossible."

These findings add to the growing puzzle from JWST, which has repeatedly found unexpectedly massive and mature galaxies in the early universe. If these galaxies contain many more small stars than thought, our models of galaxy formation need to account for how such huge numbers of stars appeared so soon after the Big Bang.

The implications could extend beyond galaxy formation. More stars could mean more planets, potentially increasing the chances for life in the early universe. As JWST continues to observe, we may uncover even more surprises about our cosmic origins.
why_it_matters: This challenges core models of how the universe evolved, which affects how we understand our own cosmic origins and the potential for life elsewhere.

background_read: The James Webb Space Telescope, a NASA-led infrared space observatory launched in 2021, can detect faint light from the early universe that older telescopes could not see clearly.

The Very Large Telescope is a set of four large ground-based telescopes in Chile operated by the European Southern Observatory; it added supporting observations of the same galaxies in different wavelengths.
Penn State, a major public university in the United States, has researchers who build models of how stars and galaxies form.
Earlier work with the Hubble Space Telescope had led many astronomers to expect young galaxies to be relatively small and chemically simple.
JWST has repeatedly upset that picture by finding galaxies that appear too massive, too mature, or too structured for their age, forcing scientists to revisit the timeline of the early universe.
Because bright stars outshine faint ones, mass estimates based only on light can be misleading.

perspectives.description: Astronomers see this as an exciting chance to improve long-standing galaxy formation models. If hidden low-mass stars are common, new physics or better star-formation histories may explain how galaxies grew so quickly.
The finding challenges previous assumptions and may mean some accepted timelines or mass estimates were wrong. That uncertainty could weaken confidence in other conclusions about the early universe.

JWST is repeatedly producing data that do not fit earlier models, which is a classic pattern of scientific revision. Researchers will need to separate real hidden stellar populations from errors in brightness-to-mass calculations.
Future JWST surveys and simulations will test whether these early galaxies truly hold many faint stars. The result could also guide searches for planets and life in the early universe.
